transformers-llm.title: How the Transformer lesson turns a model into an explorable system
transformers-llm.summary: This process explains the educational flow behind the Transformer mini app: the interface breaks a large language model into attention, tokens, layers and prediction so the user can inspect one mechanism at a time.
conceptDetails: A Transformer is the core architecture behind most modern LLMs. Its central idea is to process a token sequence and decide which parts of the context matter most for each position.
Attention lets every token look at other tokens in the context. This is how the model connects subjects, intent, long-range dependencies and meaning instead of reading text as a rigid chain.
In an LLM, many Transformer layers refine internal representations: simple patterns become more abstract relationships, then finally a probability distribution over the next token.
The mini app does not train a real Transformer; it explains the main pieces so the user understands why attention, context and prediction sit at the center of LLM behavior.
transformers-llm.runtime: React view components with local interaction state and visual diagrams.
transformers-llm.userValue: Understand how attention and layered computation produce the next-token behavior seen in LLMs.

stages.title: Frame the model
stages.description: The lesson starts by naming the Transformer as a sequence processor instead of a black box.
stages.detail: The page orients the user around tokens, context and representations before any detailed diagram appears.

stages.title: Expose attention
stages.description: Attention is shown as weighted relationships between tokens.
stages.detail: Queries, keys and values become visible concepts so the user can reason about why one token affects another.

stages.title: Stack the layers
stages.description: The app then shows how repeated blocks refine the representation.
stages.detail: Each layer adds structure: normalization, attention, feed-forward transformation and residual flow.

stages.title: Predict the token
stages.description: The final step connects internal activations to next-token probabilities.
stages.detail: The output is treated as a ranked distribution, not a single magical answer.

architecture: Static educational content defines the major Transformer concepts.
Interactive view components isolate attention, architecture, glossary and prediction examples.
Frontend state controls the currently inspected concept without requiring a backend request.
The route registry maps the AI slug to this process page and its matching explore page.
signals: The user can explain attention without relying on vague model language.
The visual flow keeps tokens, layers and prediction connected.
The concept density increases gradually instead of dumping the full architecture at once.
caveats: It is a conceptual simulator, not an exact reproduction of a production LLM.
The diagrams simplify dimensions, heads and matrix operations for readability.
The lesson should avoid implying that the largest probability is always the selected token.

web-scraping-ai.title: How a URL becomes cleaned page text and an AI summary
web-scraping-ai.summary: This process explains the two web scraping flows: a local/Ollama-backed scrape path and an OpenAI summary path. Both begin with a URL, extract readable content, then ask a model to produce a compact explanation.
conceptDetails: Web scraping is the process of reading a web page automatically to extract useful content such as title, main text, links or structured data.
When combined with AI, scraping becomes more than extraction: cleaned page text can be summarized, classified or converted from messy web content into usable knowledge.
The hard part is not only calling a URL. Many pages load content with JavaScript, block bots or mix navigation, scripts and ads with the relevant text.
The mini app shows that chain: URL, HTML download, parser cleanup, browser fallback when needed and model-based summarization.
web-scraping-ai.runtime: Frontend form, Axios API client, Express routes, Axios/Cheerio scraping, optional Playwright fallback and LLM completion.
web-scraping-ai.userValue: See the real backend path between a web page, extracted text and generated summary.

stages.title: Submit URL
stages.description: The user enters a URL and the frontend validates that it is not empty.
stages.detail: React Query starts the mutation, progress labels move through request, scrape, cleanup and summary states.

stages.title: Fetch document
stages.description: The backend requests the page with browser-like headers.
stages.detail: Static HTML is attempted first because it is faster and cheaper than launching a browser.

stages.title: Extract text
stages.description: Cheerio removes scripts, styles and noisy elements, then normalizes body text.
stages.detail: If the result is too short, the backend can use Playwright for dynamic pages that need rendering.

stages.title: Summarize
stages.description: The cleaned content is sent to Ollama or OpenAI with a focused summarization prompt.
stages.detail: The response returns title, URL, content preview, summary and runtime metrics.

architecture: Ollama flow: frontend calls /summarized-website and the backend uses the OpenAI-compatible Ollama endpoint.
OpenAI flow: frontend calls /openai/summarized-website and the backend uses the OpenAI client.
Scraping logic is shared conceptually: request HTML, extract readable text, fallback to browser rendering when needed.
The UI separates slow backend work from user feedback with progress copy and error display.
signals: The summary includes the page title and a useful overview instead of raw scraped text only.
The backend logs identify whether the failure happened during scraping or model generation.
The frontend should surface backend error messages, not only generic Axios status text.
caveats: Some sites block scraping, require JavaScript, or return bot-protection pages.
Ollama can exceed proxy timeouts on a VPS if the model is cold or the page content is large.
Playwright browsers must be installed on the server for dynamic fallback to work.

multi-modal-ai-sdk-demos.title: How multimodal input is normalized into one AI response flow
multi-modal-ai-sdk-demos.summary: This process explains how the multimodal demo gathers different input types, converts them into a request shape the backend understands, and returns a structured AI result the interface can display.
conceptDetails: Multimodal AI works with more than one kind of information: text, images, audio, documents or metadata. The model can interpret visual or contextual signals, not only words.
The value appears when modalities combine: an image with an instruction, a file with a question, or visual content turned into description and analysis.
The architectural challenge is normalizing different inputs into a consistent request so the backend can validate them, call the right provider and return renderable output.
The mini app shows why multimodal experiences need preview UI, payload validation and structured responses instead of only free-form chat.
multi-modal-ai-sdk-demos.runtime: React controls, multipart or JSON payloads, backend validation and model calls through the AI SDK/OpenAI layer.
multi-modal-ai-sdk-demos.userValue: Understand how text, images and generated metadata can participate in one coherent AI interaction.

stages.title: Collect input
stages.description: The interface gathers text prompts and optional media.
stages.detail: Controls keep the request explicit so the user knows which modality is being tested.

stages.title: Prepare payload
stages.description: Frontend services package the input into the format expected by the backend route.
stages.detail: Files, prompt text and settings are kept separate until the API boundary.

stages.title: Model reasoning
stages.description: The backend forwards the normalized input to a model that can read the selected modalities.
stages.detail: The prompt asks for a response that is useful to render, not only free-form prose.

stages.title: Render result
stages.description: The UI displays summaries, labels, generated text and supporting metadata.
stages.detail: The result becomes inspectable so users can compare what each input type contributed.

architecture: The view owns interaction state and input preview.
A service layer hides request details from the visual component.
The backend validates payloads before calling the model provider.
The response is shaped for a dashboard-style display instead of a raw chat transcript.
signals: The response references the uploaded or selected modality directly.
Loading states make long generation feel intentional.
The result separates model output from transport or file metadata.
caveats: Large images or files can increase latency and provider cost.
Different models support different modality limits.
The UI should guard against unsupported file types before the backend receives them.

pipelines-architecture.title: How AI tasks move through provider-aware pipelines
pipelines-architecture.summary: This process explains how the pipelines mini app turns common AI tasks into a consistent backend contract. Each operation runs through validation, provider selection, execution and metadata formatting.
conceptDetails: An AI pipeline is a chain of steps that transforms input into useful output: validate data, prepare prompt, choose model, run inference, post-process and return metadata.
In LLM systems, pipelines prevent every feature from becoming an improvised model call. Summarization, classification and extraction become clear, maintainable contracts.
Pipeline architecture makes provider changes safer. The frontend asks for a task; the backend decides whether to use local logic, Hugging Face, OpenAI or another provider.
The mini app explains AI as an operational system, not as a magic button.
pipelines-architecture.runtime: React task panels, API service calls, Express pipeline routes and provider implementations.
pipelines-architecture.userValue: See how summarization, classification and generation can share one architecture without sharing one model.

stages.title: Choose task
stages.description: The user selects a pipeline such as summarization or classification.
stages.detail: The frontend keeps inputs task-specific while preserving one interaction pattern.

stages.title: Validate request
stages.description: The backend checks the shape and minimum content needed for the selected operation.
stages.detail: Invalid payloads fail early instead of reaching the provider layer.

stages.title: Run provider
stages.description: The pipeline service chooses local or external execution based on configuration.
stages.detail: Provider classes keep Hugging Face, local logic or future vendors behind the same interface.

stages.title: Return metadata
stages.description: The response includes result data plus model/provider information.
stages.detail: This helps the UI explain not only the answer, but how the answer was produced.

architecture: Frontend services expose task functions such as summarize while hiding endpoint details.
Controllers parse and validate DTOs before calling the pipeline service.
Provider implementations share a common interface so swapping execution strategies is localized.
Metadata wraps each result for observability and teaching value.
signals: The same UI pattern can run different task types.
Provider changes do not force component rewrites.
Responses include enough metadata to debug which backend path ran.
caveats: Remote providers can fail independently of frontend correctness.
Local fallbacks may be less accurate than specialized models.
Long text inputs need truncation or chunking to stay within provider limits.

tokenizer-playground.title: How raw text becomes model-countable tokens
tokenizer-playground.summary: This process explains how the tokenizer mini app turns text into tokens, classifications and cost-like metrics so users can see why wording changes model input size.
conceptDetails: Tokenization converts human text into units a model can process. A token can be a full word, a word fragment, whitespace, punctuation or a symbol.
LLMs do not see sentences the way humans do; they see sequences of token IDs. Two texts with similar character counts can consume very different context budgets.
Tokenization affects cost, latency, context limits and prompt quality. Understanding it helps users write better instructions and avoid oversized inputs.
The mini app makes the invisible visible: it shows how text is split, how tokens are counted and how those tokens affect model usage.
tokenizer-playground.runtime: Frontend text controls, tokenizer API service and backend tokenizer providers.
tokenizer-playground.userValue: Learn why characters, words and tokens are different units in LLM systems.

stages.title: Enter text
stages.description: The user writes or pastes text into the playground.
stages.detail: The UI keeps the original text visible so token boundaries can be compared against it.

stages.title: Tokenize
stages.description: The backend provider splits text using model-aware tokenization rules.
stages.detail: A fallback provider can keep the demo usable even when an external tokenizer is unavailable.

stages.title: Classify tokens
stages.description: Tokens are annotated as words, spaces, punctuation, currency, numbers or special fragments.
stages.detail: Classification gives color and meaning to what would otherwise be opaque IDs.

stages.title: Show impact
stages.description: The result exposes counts, previews and estimated usage metrics.
stages.detail: Users can edit text and immediately see how prompt shape affects token budget.

architecture: React owns text input, selected model and visualization state.
The tokenizer service sends text and model settings to the backend.
Backend providers normalize token output into a stable response type.
Formatting helpers prepare token labels and statistics for display.
signals: Token boundaries align with the selected model behavior.
Counts update predictably when text changes.
Special cases such as whitespace, currency and punctuation remain visible.
caveats: Fallback tokenization is educational and may not match provider token IDs exactly.
Different models use different vocabularies and merge rules.
Very large inputs should be bounded before visualization.

quantization-playground.title: How precision changes model size, speed and error
quantization-playground.summary: This process explains the quantization playground: the app simulates compressing model values into lower precision formats and shows the tradeoff between memory savings and reconstruction error.
conceptDetails: Quantization reduces the numeric precision of model weights or activations, for example moving from 32-bit values to 16-bit, 8-bit or even smaller formats.
For LLMs, this can make larger models runnable with less memory and lower cost, especially on smaller GPUs, CPUs or edge environments.
The tradeoff is error: compressed numbers are less exact. With good calibration the quality drop can be small; with poor settings it can damage answers, reasoning or stability.
The mini app shows that model optimization is not only making things smaller; it means comparing savings, precision, error and deployment consequences.
quantization-playground.runtime: React controls, compression hook, quantization service and result visualization.
quantization-playground.userValue: Understand why smaller numeric precision can make models cheaper to run while changing output quality.

stages.title: Select precision
stages.description: The user chooses source and target formats such as FP32, FP16 or INT8-like compression.
stages.detail: Controls make the tradeoff explicit before the calculation starts.

stages.title: Compress values
stages.description: The service maps sample weights into the selected lower precision representation.
stages.detail: The app treats quantization as a measurable transformation, not an abstract optimization word.

stages.title: Compare result
stages.description: Original and quantized values are compared for error and storage impact.
stages.detail: Metrics show compression ratio, estimated memory and reconstruction difference.

stages.title: Explain tradeoff
stages.description: The UI translates numeric results into deployment consequences.
stages.detail: Users can connect lower memory use with possible quality loss and faster inference.

architecture: Frontend controls define the compression scenario.
A hook manages the request lifecycle and progress display.
The backend quantization module computes result metrics.
Result cards separate precision, compression and quality information.
signals: Users can see both savings and error in the same view.
Changing precision changes metrics in an understandable way.
The explanation connects math to deployment concerns.
caveats: The demo simplifies production quantization algorithms.
Real model quality depends on calibration data and architecture.
Compression ratio alone is not enough to judge deployment success.

embeddings-lab.title: How text becomes searchable vector meaning
embeddings-lab.summary: This process explains how the embeddings lab sends text to an embedding provider, receives vectors, then uses distance and grouping operations to make semantic similarity visible.
conceptDetails: An embedding is a numeric representation of meaning. The model converts text, documents or phrases into vectors where distance reflects semantic similarity.
This enables search by meaning instead of exact keywords. Two different sentences can be close if they express the same idea.
Embeddings power semantic search, clustering, recommendations and RAG, where relevant context is retrieved before calling an LLM.
The mini app shows how to generate vectors, compare them with cosine similarity and understand why semantic search finds relationships text filters miss.
embeddings-lab.runtime: React panels, embedding hooks, backend embedding providers and similarity utilities.
embeddings-lab.userValue: Learn how semantic search compares meaning through vectors instead of exact keyword matching.

stages.title: Provide text
stages.description: The user enters queries, documents or groups of short texts.
stages.detail: Each panel focuses on a different embedding workflow: generate, compare, search or group.

stages.title: Generate vectors
stages.description: The backend provider transforms text into numeric embeddings.
stages.detail: The frontend never needs to understand vector dimensions to use the result.

stages.title: Measure similarity
stages.description: Cosine similarity or related scoring compares vectors.
stages.detail: Scores make semantic closeness visible even when words do not exactly match.

stages.title: Render insight
stages.description: The UI shows matches, clusters or comparison rankings.
stages.detail: The user can inspect why one text is closer to another in the embedding space.

architecture: Multiple panels reuse the same embedding service through specialized hooks.
The backend chooses local or external embedding providers from environment configuration.
Service responses normalize vectors, scores and metadata for the UI.
The interface keeps raw vector mechanics secondary to semantic interpretation.
signals: Semantically similar texts rank higher even with different wording.
Scores are displayed alongside human-readable labels.
Provider metadata helps debug which embedding model produced the vectors.
caveats: Embeddings can encode provider bias and domain mismatch.
Similarity scores are relative, not universal truth.
Large document sets need indexing rather than one-off comparison.

autoregressive-inference-token-by-token.title: How generation unfolds one token at a time
autoregressive-inference-token-by-token.summary: This process explains autoregressive inference by showing how a prompt becomes a loop: tokenize context, predict the next token, append it, and repeat until the generation stops.
conceptDetails: Autoregressive inference is how an LLM generates text sequentially. The model does not write the whole answer at once; it predicts the next token again and again.
Every generated token is appended to the context, and that new context changes the next prediction. This is why the output takes shape step by step.
Settings such as temperature, top-k or top-p influence how much variety the model accepts when choosing among likely tokens.
The mini app explains generation as an observable loop: context, distribution, selection, append and next prediction.
autoregressive-inference-token-by-token.runtime: React generation controls, token preview panels and token inference backend service.
autoregressive-inference-token-by-token.userValue: Understand why LLM output is sequential and why each generated token changes the next prediction.

stages.title: Prepare context
stages.description: The prompt is tokenized and displayed as the starting context.
stages.detail: Users can see that generation begins with existing tokens, not an empty state.

stages.title: Predict next token
stages.description: The model scores possible continuations based on the current context.
stages.detail: The demo can compare normal generation with a streaming-like step sequence.

stages.title: Append output
stages.description: The selected token is added to the context.
stages.detail: This new context becomes the input for the next prediction loop.

stages.title: Stop generation
stages.description: The loop ends when it reaches a limit, stop signal or completed response.
stages.detail: The UI makes stopping conditions visible so generation feels deterministic enough to reason about.

architecture: Controls define prompt, temperature-like settings and generation mode.
The token inference service coordinates backend calls.
Preview panels separate tokenization, normal generation and streaming generation.
Token chips provide a small visual unit for each step in the sequence.
signals: Each step visibly depends on the tokens before it.
Streaming output is explained as repeated prediction, not a different kind of intelligence.
The user can compare prompt changes against generated continuation changes.
caveats: The demo may use local or simplified inference rather than a full production model.
Sampling behavior can be non-deterministic depending on configuration.
Long generations need limits to avoid slow or expensive requests.

token-prediction.title: How next-token probabilities become an inspectable prediction path
token-prediction.summary: This process explains the token prediction mini app: the backend calculates likely next tokens and the frontend turns the distribution into cards, timelines, paths and tree-like explanations.
conceptDetails: Next-token prediction is the operating core of LLMs. Given a context, the model assigns probability to many possible next tokens.
The real output is not one inevitable word; it is a distribution. Some continuations are highly likely, some are possible but rare and others are nearly impossible.
Visualizing this distribution helps explain uncertainty, creativity, alternative completions and why small prompt changes can shift the output.
The mini app turns an abstract operation into something inspectable: candidates, ranking, probability, path and branches.
token-prediction.runtime: React prediction visualizers, token prediction hook and backend prediction providers.
token-prediction.userValue: Learn that language models choose from a probability distribution, not from a single scripted answer.

stages.title: Send context
stages.description: The user provides a phrase or prompt fragment.
stages.detail: The phrase becomes the context used to score likely next tokens.

stages.title: Score candidates
stages.description: The provider returns top token candidates and probability-like values.
stages.detail: The result exposes alternatives so uncertainty is visible.

stages.title: Build path
stages.description: The frontend organizes candidates into cards, timeline steps and prediction branches.
stages.detail: Different visualizations tell the same probability story from different angles.

stages.title: Explain choice
stages.description: Stats and labels help users understand why one continuation is more likely than another.
stages.detail: The UI focuses on reasoning about ranking, confidence and branching.

architecture: The hook manages request state and prediction data.
The backend provider abstracts local or OpenAI-backed prediction logic.
View components split distribution cards, tree, timeline, path and stats.
The app keeps prompt input close to the resulting probability explanation.
signals: Top candidates are easy to compare.
The visual path reflects probability differences without hiding alternatives.
Stats make uncertainty legible instead of presenting a single answer as inevitable.
caveats: Probability values can vary by provider and sampling settings.
Top-k views only show a slice of the full vocabulary.
Prediction demos should avoid implying that language models understand intent perfectly.
